stem.text: The proton (1H) NMR spectra of three compounds, P, Q and R, are shown in Figure 8.1. The solvent used is CDCl3 in each case.

stem.caption: Figure 8.1
stem.alt: Three proton NMR spectra, chemical shift δ/ppm on each x-axis. Compound P: a quartet near 3.7, a singlet near 2.6, a triplet near 1.2 and a small peak at 0. Compound Q: clusters of peaks between about 6.8 and 7.3, a singlet near 5.4 and a small peak at 0. Compound R: a small broad peak near 11.5, a tall singlet near 2.1 and a small peak at 0.

stem.text: Identify the substance responsible for the peak at δ = 0 ppm on each spectrum.

explanation.text: Tetramethylsilane is added as the reference standard. Its 12 equivalent protons give one sharp singlet, defined as δ = 0 ppm, and it is inert, volatile and absorbs upfield of almost all organic protons.

reasoningChain: A peak at exactly δ = 0 in every spectrum is the reference.

inferredMistakes.text: Naming the solvent CDCl<sub>3</sub>, which has no <sup>1</sup>H and is not the δ = 0 reference.
Writing an incorrect formula such as Si(CH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>4</sub> or (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>C.

stem.text: P, Q and R are phenol, ethanol and ethanoic acid, but not necessarily in this order.
Explain your answer, identifying the protons responsible for the peaks in the relevant spectrum.

guidance: I Q and 4 peaks for 4 (proton) environments (question asks for protons responsible).
If explanation is blank, check spectra.

explanation.text: Only Q has peaks in the aromatic region (6.8–7.3 ppm, H–Ar range 6.0–9.0), so only Q contains a benzene ring. Its other peak, at 5.4 ppm, lies in the phenol O–H range (4.5–7.0). Each mark needs both the letter Q and a peak assigned to its type of proton.
For comparison, R has a broad peak near 11.5 (RCOOH) and a singlet near 2.1 (CH<sub>3</sub>–C=O): ethanoic acid. P has a quartet, singlet and triplet: ethanol.

reasoningChain: Look for the aromatic region (6–9 ppm): only Q has peaks there.
Assign Q’s 6.8–7.3 ppm peaks to H–Ar.
Assign Q’s 5.4 ppm peak to Ar–OH.

inferredMistakes.text: Explaining only by the number of peaks or environments, without assigning protons to peaks; the MS ignores this.
Assigning the 5.4 ppm peak to an alkene proton (=CHR also falls in 4.5–6.0).
Giving peak assignments without stating that Q is phenol, so neither mark can be awarded.

stem.text: The spectrum of P has peaks at δ = 1.2 ppm and δ = 3.7 ppm.
Name the splitting pattern of each of these peaks and give a reason why the peaks are split in this way.

labels: splitting pattern of the peak at δ = 1.2 ppm
splitting pattern of the peak at δ = 3.7 ppm

guidance: A neighbouring CH2 or CH3 for adjacent.
A near-miss spellings (e.g. one letter missing / incorrect only or ‘tirplet’, etc.).

explanation.text: P is ethanol, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH. The peak at 1.2 ppm is the CH<sub>3</sub>; its neighbouring carbon is the CH<sub>2</sub> with 2 H, so by the n + 1 rule it is a triplet. The peak at 3.7 ppm is the CH<sub>2</sub> next to O; its neighbouring carbon carries 3 H, so it is a quartet. The OH proton (singlet near 2.6) does not split the CH<sub>2</sub> because it exchanges rapidly.
Two of the four points earn one mark; all four earn two. The reason must say the protons are on the adjacent carbon.

reasoningChain: Assign 1.2 ppm to CH<sub>3</sub> and 3.7 ppm to CH<sub>2</sub>–O.
CH<sub>3</sub>: 2 H on next C, n + 1 = 3, triplet.
CH<sub>2</sub>: 3 H on next C, n + 1 = 4, quartet.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving the number of H on the carbon itself as the reason (e.g. ‘triplet because CH<sub>3</sub> has 3 H’).
Swapping the two patterns, calling the 1.2 ppm peak a quartet.
Including the OH proton as a neighbour of the CH<sub>2</sub> and predicting a quintet.

stem.text: The spectrum of Q dissolved in D2O is obtained.
Describe how this spectrum differs from the spectrum of Q shown in Figure 8.1.

guidance: I it would have 3 or 4 peaks as we don’t know if they are counting the TMS peak.

points.text:
peak (at 5.4) disappears and
the OH / 5.4 proton / H is liaible or
the OH / 5.4 proton / H exchanges / replaced with D or
equation, e.g. ROH + D2O → ROD + DHO

explanation.text: In D<sub>2</sub>O the labile O–H proton of phenol exchanges with deuterium: C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + D<sub>2</sub>O ⇌ C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OD + HDO. Deuterium gives no signal in a <sup>1</sup>H spectrum, so the O–H peak at 5.4 ppm disappears; the aromatic peaks stay.
The explanation must say the H atom is exchanged for a D atom. ‘OH exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O’ or ‘reacts with D<sub>2</sub>O’ is ignored because it does not say what is swapped.

reasoningChain: Identify the exchangeable proton in Q: the O–H at 5.4 ppm.
D is invisible in <sup>1</sup>H NMR, so the 5.4 ppm peak disappears.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying the number of peaks changes, without identifying which peak goes; the MS ignores this.
Writing ‘the OH group exchanges with D<sub>2</sub>O’ rather than ‘the H exchanges with D’.
Saying the aromatic peaks disappear, which contradicts the answer.

stem.text: Compare the acidities of phenol, ethanol and ethanoic acid.

guidance: A ecf for matching O–H strength / anion stability correctly to incorrect order for bullet 1.
CON bullet 1 for incorrect reference to O–H bond strength / anion stability.
I COOH / COO– is an electron withdrawing group.
A e– / negative charge delocalises over COO– / C=O.

points.text: correct reference to O-H bond strength / anion stability
(ethanoic acid) C=O has electron withdrawing / –I effect
(phenol) LP/p-orbital on O overlaps/is delocalised and with/into ring/π system

markScheme.note: The MS prints the order ‘ethanoic acid     phenol     ethanol’ on its own line, then four bullets, then ‘⚫ ✓ ✓ ✓ for four bullets’. Point 1 is the order; points 2–5 are the four bullets.

explanation.text: Acidity depends on how easily the O–H breaks to release H<sup>+</sup>, which is linked to how stable the anion is. Ethanoic acid is the strongest: the electron-withdrawing C=O weakens the O–H bond, and the negative charge of ethanoate is delocalised over both O atoms of COO<sup>–</sup>.

Phenol comes next: a lone pair (p orbital) on the O overlaps with the ring π system, which draws electron density from O, weakens O–H and spreads the charge of phenoxide into the ring. Ethanol is the weakest: the ethyl group donates electrons (+I), strengthening O–H and destabilising ethoxide.
Give the order on the answer line first, then explain each compound separately: the MS has one bullet for the general O–H/anion idea and one for each compound.

reasoningChain: General idea: weaker O–H / more stable anion means stronger acid.
Ethanoic acid: C=O electron-withdrawing, charge delocalised over COO<sup>–</sup>.
Phenol: O lone pair delocalised into the ring.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying the phenol ring is electron-withdrawing without mentioning the lone pair or p orbital on O overlapping with the π system.
Saying ‘COOH is an electron-withdrawing group’ rather than pointing to the C=O; the MS ignores this.
Linking a stronger O–H bond to a stronger acid, which contradicts the first bullet.
Putting phenol above ethanoic acid because it has a benzene ring.

issues.note: MS 原文 'liaible'（应为 labile）照抄。
MS 只印 '⚫ ✓ ✓ ✓ for four bullets'，没有写明排序是否单独给分。4 分可能是：排序 1 分 + 四个 bullet 3 分（四个 bullet 中前几个给 1 分？），也可能 '⚫' 表示第 1 个 bullet 不单独给分。站内把排序作为 point 1，四个 bullet 作为 points 2–5，不加解释，请 owner 核对给分方式。
Guidance 第一条 'I Q and 4 peaks for 4 (proton) environments (question asks for protons responsible).' 原文跨三行，拼成一句。
表中 –CH2–Cl 的 Cl 原文是正体 Cl（不是 CDCl3 那样的斜体 l），照原样。
跨章题：(a)–(c) 是 37.4 质子 NMR，(d) 是 32.2/33.1 酸性比较。NMR 占 6 分，放在第 37 章 Analytical techniques 的 Cross-topic。
